library-a-tiny-seed-page-00-3: Nicola Rijsdijk & Maya Marshak Little Island Library adaptation.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-01-1: In a village on the slopes of Mount Kenya in East Africa, a little girl worked in the fields with her mother.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-02-2: In her family’s food garden she broke up the soil with her machete.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-02-3: She pressed tiny seeds into the warm earth.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-03-1: Her favourite time of day was just after sunset.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-03-2: When it got too dark to see the plants, Wangari knew it was time to go home.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-03-3: She would follow the narrow paths through the fields, crossing rivers as she went.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-04-review: Wangari’s big brother asked why she did not go to school with him. Her mother agreed to send her. Wangari later said she loved learning to read and write.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-05-2: Wangari learnt more and more with every book she read.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-05-3: She did so well at school that she was invited to study in the United States of America.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-05-5: She wanted to know more about the world.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-06-1: At the American university Wangari learnt many new things.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-06-2: She studied plants and how they grow.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-06-3: And she remembered how she grew: playing games with her brothers in the shade of the trees in the beautiful Kenyan forests.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-07-1: The more she learnt, the more she realised that she loved the people of Kenya.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-07-2: She wanted them to be happy and free.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-07-3: The more she learnt, the more she remembered her African home.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-08-review: After her studies, Wangari returned to Kenya. She listened to rural women who needed firewood, food and clean water. Trees and streams that their families relied on were being lost.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-09-review: Wangari worked with women to grow and plant trees. Their work became the Green Belt Movement. Together, they cared for the land and worked to improve life in their communities.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-10-review: The movement grew. Women and their communities planted millions of trees in Kenya. People in other African countries took up the idea too.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-11-2: People all over the world took notice, and gave her a famous prize.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-11-3: It is called the Nobel Peace Prize, and she was the first African woman ever to receive it.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-12-1: Wangari died in 2011, but we can think of her every time we see a beautiful tree.

library-airplanes-deep-1: An airplane needs forces that support it and keep it moving.
library-airplanes-deep-10: Engines help overcome drag, while the wing’s interaction with moving air produces most of the lift.
library-airplanes-deep-2: Air flowing around a wing changes direction, producing a force on the wing in the opposite direction.
library-airplanes-deep-3: In level flight, this gives the upward lift that balances weight.
library-airplanes-deep-4: Both the upper and lower wing surfaces help turn the flow; thinking only about air hitting the bottom misses part of the explanation.
library-airplanes-deep-5: Meanwhile, drag resists motion and the engine provides thrust.

library-asteroids-deep-3: Many of those rocky bodies now orbit in the main asteroid belt.
library-asteroids-deep-4: They are separate objects following paths around the Sun, rather than one solid band.
library-asteroids-deep-5: Their surfaces and materials record different histories.
library-asteroids-deep-6: Some contain clay and rocky minerals, while others contain much more metal.
library-asteroids-deep-7: Collisions can leave craters, and many asteroids have lumpy shapes.
library-asteroids-deep-9: Spacecraft images and measurements let scientists compare these clues instead of treating every asteroid as the same kind of rock.

library-astronaut-home-deep-8: Without the usual loads of life on Earth, bones and muscles can weaken, so exercise is part of the crew’s routine.
library-astronaut-home-deep-9: Floating may look effortless, yet keeping people healthy and supplied requires carefully designed equipment and daily work.

library-bats-deep-10: Researchers can study these mostly unheard calls with special microphones and turn them into visible sound patterns.
library-bats-deep-2: Muscles move this structure to produce powered flight.
library-bats-deep-3: That makes bats different from mammals such as flying squirrels, which glide rather than sustain flight by flapping.
library-bats-deep-4: Wing shape is only part of the story.
library-bats-deep-5: Bats have hair and feed their young milk, the mammal traits that explain why a flying animal is not automatically a bird.

library-bats-deep-7: They send out calls and listen as the sound returns from nearby objects.
library-bats-deep-8: Those echoes help them navigate and locate food in darkness.

library-beach-sand-deep-1: Sand forms when larger material becomes small grains, but those grains do not all start in the same place.
library-beach-sand-deep-10: Thus, a beach’s color can reflect both the rocks around it and the living things that supplied its grains.
library-beach-sand-deep-2: Rain, weathering and erosion break rocks down on land.
library-beach-sand-deep-3: Rivers and streams carry pieces, wearing them further as they travel.
library-beach-sand-deep-4: At the coast, waves and tides continue the process.
library-beach-sand-deep-5: A grain may have traveled far before reaching a beach.
library-beach-sand-deep-6: Its material helps explain its color: dark volcanic rock can supply black sand, while quartz and feldspar contribute to many tan beaches.
library-beach-sand-deep-8: Shells and coral skeletons can break into grains, and some parrotfish grind swallowed reef material into sand.

library-bees-deep-10: The bee does not have to plan to help the flower; its own food-gathering trip can make the transfer happen.
library-bees-deep-2: A visiting bee can provide that journey while searching for food.
library-bees-deep-3: The flower's anthers produce pollen, and its stigma is a surface where pollen can land.
library-bees-deep-4: As a bee brushes past an anther, grains can cling to its body.
library-bees-deep-5: Some may rub onto a stigma during another visit.
library-bees-deep-6: This transfer is pollination, a step many flowering plants need before making seeds.
library-bees-deep-7: Often the pollen must come from the same kind of plant, rather than any flower nearby.
library-bees-deep-8: The bee benefits too: nectar provides sugary food, and pollen supplies nutrients.

library-bicycle-deep-2: The pedals turn cranks and a front chainring, whose teeth engage the chain.
library-bicycle-deep-3: The chain carries motion to a rear cog.
library-bicycle-deep-4: Comparing their tooth counts tells us how many wheel turns follow one pedal turn.
library-bicycle-deep-5: For example, a front ring with forty teeth moving a twenty-tooth rear cog carries enough chain past to turn that cog twice.
library-bicycle-deep-6: A lower gear gives fewer wheel turns per pedal turn, helping reduce the force needed on a hill while requiring more turns for the same distance.
library-bicycle-deep-7: The bicycle has not gained free energy; the rider has changed the force-and-distance trade.
library-bicycle-deep-8: Early high-wheel bicycles worked differently, with pedals attached directly to the front wheel.
library-bicycle-deep-9: The chain allowed the rider to sit between two wheels instead.

library-bird-feathers-deep-1: A feather's jobs come from how its branching parts fit together.
library-bird-feathers-deep-10: These different jobs depend on tiny changes in feather parts that are too small to notice in a distant bird.
library-bird-feathers-deep-2: Many feathers have a central shaft with branches called barbs.
library-bird-feathers-deep-3: These carry even smaller branches called barbules.
library-bird-feathers-deep-4: In a flight feather, tiny hooks join neighboring barbules, helping form a smooth, flexible surface that works in the moving air.
library-bird-feathers-deep-5: Tail feathers with a similar structure help steer.
library-bird-feathers-deep-6: Down feathers are different: their loose branching traps air near the warm body and slows heat loss.
library-bird-feathers-deep-7: Other body feathers overlap, with exposed tips and softer bases tucked underneath.
library-bird-feathers-deep-8: A bird can therefore have several feather designs working together rather than one kind repeated everywhere.
library-bird-feathers-deep-9: Color and pattern can also help it display or blend into a background.

library-blue-sky-deep-1: The daytime sky is filled with sunlight that has changed direction.
library-blue-sky-deep-2: Sunlight contains many colors, which correspond to different wavelengths.
library-blue-sky-deep-3: Molecules in the atmosphere scatter short wavelengths, including blue, more strongly than longer red wavelengths.
library-blue-sky-deep-4: Blue light therefore reaches our eyes from many directions across the sky.
library-blue-sky-deep-5: At sunset, sunlight has a longer path through air before it reaches an observer.
library-blue-sky-deep-6: More blue is scattered out of the direct path, leaving a greater share of reds and yellows in the light that continues through.
library-blue-sky-deep-7: The Sun has not changed into a different kind of star; the air has changed the mixture of light arriving.
library-blue-sky-deep-8: Mars offers a way to test this explanation.
library-blue-sky-deep-9: Its thin, dusty atmosphere scatters light differently, and rover pictures show a bluish glow near the setting Sun rather than Earth's familiar sunset colors.

library-boats-float-deep-1: Water pressure acts on a boat from different directions, with a net upward push called buoyancy.
library-boats-float-deep-2: Archimedes’ principle says that this push equals the weight of the water displaced.
library-boats-float-deep-3: A floating boat settles until the displaced water weighs as much as the boat and everything it carries.
library-boats-float-deep-4: A steel hull can float because its hollow shape encloses a large volume without filling that whole volume with heavy material.
library-boats-float-deep-5: The average density of boat and contents can therefore be lower than water’s.
library-boats-float-deep-6: Adding cargo increases weight, so the hull sits deeper and displaces more water.
library-boats-float-deep-7: If too much is added, or water fills the hull, it may sink.
library-boats-float-deep-8: Even floating is only part of the problem: a boat can tip.
library-boats-float-deep-9: Shape affects both support and stability, which is why a lump and a hollow hull behave differently.

library-boats-float-more-2: A hollow hull has room for air, so even a metal boat can have a low average density.

library-bones-deep-1: Bones must provide support while remaining living parts of the body.
library-bones-deep-10: Bones are active organs, not dry sticks hidden inside us.
library-bones-deep-2: Their tissues need nutrients, oxygen and a blood supply.
library-bones-deep-3: Bone is continually remodeled: some material is removed and new material replaces it.
library-bones-deep-4: During childhood, new bone is added faster as the skeleton grows.
library-bones-deep-5: Its different shapes suit different jobs.
library-bones-deep-6: The skull surrounds the brain, while the rib cage helps protect organs in the chest.
library-bones-deep-7: Bones also act as levers when muscles pull on them, so a skeleton supports movement as well as stillness.
library-bones-deep-8: Inside some bones, red marrow makes blood cells.
library-bones-deep-9: The hard framework we usually think of as holding us up also contains tissue that helps renew the blood.

library-breathing-deep-1: Breathing works with circulation to exchange gases between air and the body.
library-breathing-deep-2: When the diaphragm, a muscle below the lungs, contracts, it moves down and increases space in the chest.
library-breathing-deep-3: Air enters and travels to tiny sacs called alveoli.
library-breathing-deep-4: Thin walls separate these sacs from small blood vessels.
library-breathing-deep-5: Oxygen crosses into blood, while carbon dioxide crosses from blood into the sacs.
library-breathing-deep-6: Red blood cells carry much of the oxygen using a protein called hemoglobin.
library-breathing-deep-7: The heart sends this blood onward, and cells use the oxygen as they release energy.
library-breathing-deep-8: Carbon dioxide returns in blood to the lungs and leaves in an outgoing breath.
library-breathing-deep-9: A breath therefore does more than fill and empty a space: it refreshes the gases that blood exchanges with the body’s cells.

library-breathing-more-2: Breathing brings oxygen into the lungs and lets carbon dioxide leave.
library-breathing-more-3: Blood carries the gases between lungs and cells.

library-butterflies-deep-3: Its job in this part of life is to feed and grow, often on a particular kind of host plant.
library-butterflies-deep-4: A monarch caterpillar, for example, eats milkweed leaves.
library-butterflies-deep-5: When the larva reaches the next stage, it becomes a pupa and undergoes a major transformation called complete metamorphosis.
library-butterflies-deep-6: The adult that emerges has a different body and a different way of feeding.
library-butterflies-deep-7: A monarch adult uncoils a long mouthpart to sip nectar from flowers, then curls it away again.
library-butterflies-deep-8: These changes connect body form with what the animal does at each stage.
library-butterflies-deep-9: The leaf-eating crawler and the flower-visiting flier are the same kind of animal at different times in its life.

library-clouds-deep-11: New droplets form while others disappear, so it is an ongoing process rather than a fixed object.

library-comet-deep-2: Far from the Sun it can remain relatively quiet, but warming nearer the Sun releases gas and dusty material.

library-comet-deep-4: Sunlight and the solar wind act on the escaping material to form tails.

library-constellation-deep-1: A constellation can mean a familiar star picture, but astronomers use the word more precisely for a region of sky.
library-constellation-deep-2: Eighty-eight official regions cover the sky, with agreed boundaries.
library-constellation-deep-3: An object can be described as being in one of these regions even if it is not part of the picture’s bright star pattern.
library-constellation-deep-4: This gives astronomers a shared way to describe locations.
library-constellation-deep-5: The drawn lines are a guide for people, not connections between stars.
library-constellation-deep-6: Stars that appear side by side can lie at very different distances from Earth.
library-constellation-deep-7: For example, a pattern that looks flat on paper represents a view into deep space.
library-constellation-deep-8: Even the stick figure drawn within an official region can vary between charts.
library-constellation-deep-9: The region’s boundary is standardized; one particular imagined picture does not have to be.

library-continents-deep-1: A continent is a broad way of grouping Earth's land, so counting continents involves choices as well as coastlines.
library-continents-deep-2: Many students learn a seven-continent model, but other systems combine some of those regions.
library-continents-deep-3: Europe and Asia provide a useful example.
library-continents-deep-4: Their land is continuous, yet historical and political conventions often treat them as separate continents.
library-continents-deep-5: Grouping them as Eurasia changes the count without changing a single mountain or shore.
library-continents-deep-6: Tectonic plates describe something different: moving pieces of Earth's outer shell, including both land and seafloor.
library-continents-deep-7: A continent's label is therefore not a map of one separate plate.
library-continents-deep-8: Flat world maps introduce another complication, because every projection changes some shapes, areas, distances, or directions.
library-continents-deep-9: Two maps can look different without disagreeing about where the land is; they may use different groupings or different ways to flatten a globe.

library-coral-deep-1: Coral can look like a plant or a rock because the living animal stays attached in one place.
library-coral-deep-10: An animal can rely heavily on sunlight without becoming a plant: its resident algae capture that energy for the partnership.
library-coral-deep-2: Look closer and its feeding method reveals the difference: a polyp uses tentacles to catch food from the water.
library-coral-deep-3: Many polyps live together in a colony.
library-coral-deep-4: Hard corals add skeletons made of calcium carbonate, building on older skeletons over many generations.
library-coral-deep-5: That slow construction helps form a reef's framework.
library-coral-deep-6: Many shallow-water corals also house tiny algae inside their tissues.
library-coral-deep-7: The algae use sunlight to make food through photosynthesis and share useful products with their host.
library-coral-deep-8: In return, the coral provides a protected place and materials the algae use.
library-coral-deep-9: This close partnership is called symbiosis.

library-crab-shells-deep-1: A crab’s hard covering is called an exoskeleton, meaning a skeleton on the outside.
library-crab-shells-deep-2: That covering creates a growth problem: the crab cannot simply stretch it as its body gets bigger.
library-crab-shells-deep-3: Before shedding, the crab prepares a soft replacement underneath.
library-crab-shells-deep-4: It takes in water, the old covering splits, and the crab pulls its body free.
library-crab-shells-deep-5: While the new covering is soft, it can expand before becoming hard protection again.
library-crab-shells-deep-6: A shed covering may still have the shapes of legs and eyes, so it can look surprisingly like a whole crab.
library-crab-shells-deep-7: A hermit crab has another covering as well: a snail shell it moves into.
library-crab-shells-deep-8: This borrowed shell shelters its softer rear body.
library-crab-shells-deep-9: Changing that shelter and shedding its own exoskeleton are two different parts of a hermit crab’s life.
library-crab-shells-more-1: A crab’s hard outer coat supports and protects its body, but it cannot grow along with it.
library-crab-shells-more-2: The crab makes a soft new coat underneath, then works its way out of the old one.
library-crab-shells-more-3: The new coat expands and hardens.
library-crab-shells-more-4: Give a growing crab room; let it keep its shelter.
library-crab-shells-tell-1: A crab has a hard coat.
library-crab-shells-tell-2: It sheds the coat so it can grow.
library-day-night-deep-1: Earth's daily turning carries the place where you live into sunlight and then away from it.
library-day-night-deep-2: The imaginary line it turns around is its axis, which runs through the North and South Poles.
library-day-night-deep-3: At any moment, the Sun lights roughly half the planet.
library-day-night-deep-4: A place on the lit side has daytime; a place turned away has nighttime.
library-day-night-deep-5: Turning a marked globe beside a fixed light makes this change easier to follow.
library-day-night-deep-6: The mark moves even though the light stays in place.
library-day-night-deep-7: Earth also travels around the Sun, but that larger journey takes about a year.
library-day-night-deep-8: It is a different motion from the spin that makes our daily pattern.
library-day-night-deep-9: Earth keeps doing both at once: while your home turns through one day, the whole planet also moves along its yearly path.

library-deep-ocean-deep-1: Deep water creates two separate challenges for exploration.
library-deep-ocean-deep-10: Darkness does not mean emptiness: deep-sea animals live where our familiar source of daylight never reaches them.
library-deep-ocean-deep-2: First, the weight of the water above produces hydrostatic pressure, a push spread over an area.
library-deep-ocean-deep-3: The farther down a vehicle travels, the greater that pressure becomes.
library-deep-ocean-deep-4: It acts from all directions, including the sides and underneath, so a strong roof alone would not protect a research cabin.
library-deep-ocean-deep-5: Second, sunlight fades as it travels through water.
library-deep-ocean-deep-6: In the deepest zones, none arrives from the surface.
library-deep-ocean-deep-7: Researchers therefore use specially designed vehicles and instruments, including robots with lights and pressure-resistant parts.
library-deep-ocean-deep-8: Some vehicles carry people; others are controlled from a distance.
library-deep-ocean-deep-9: A photograph taken there is the result of solving both problems together.

library-directions-deep-1: North can mean different things on a map, which is why some maps show several arrows.
library-directions-deep-2: True north follows a line of longitude toward the geographic North Pole.
library-directions-deep-3: Magnetic north shows the direction a compass points at a particular place and time.
library-directions-deep-4: Those directions can differ, and the angle between them is called magnetic declination.
library-directions-deep-5: It changes with location and over time, so an old map's magnetic information may no longer be correct.
library-directions-deep-6: Grid north follows the straight coordinate lines used on the flat map.
library-directions-deep-7: Flattening Earth's curved surface can leave this direction slightly different from true north too.

library-distant-stars-deep-1: A star’s real width and the width it seems to have in our sky are different measurements.
library-distant-stars-deep-2: With enough distance, a huge star covers only a tiny angle in our view.
library-distant-stars-deep-3: Our eyes cannot separate its edges, so we see a point of light rather than a visible disk.
library-distant-stars-deep-4: Even most backyard telescopes leave distant stars looking like points.
library-distant-stars-deep-5: The Sun appears much larger because it is our nearest star.
library-distant-stars-deep-6: Other stars can be larger or smaller than the Sun, so appearance alone cannot tell us their real size.
library-distant-stars-deep-8: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, not a measure of age.
library-distant-stars-deep-9: Light from a star several light-years away began its journey years before we see it.
library-distant-stars-more-1: The Sun is a star, but it is far closer to Earth than other stars.
library-distant-stars-more-2: Distant stars take up such a tiny part of our view that we cannot make out their round shapes.
library-distant-stars-more-3: They look like points even though they are enormous objects.
library-distant-stars-tell-2: Most look like dots to us.
library-dolphins-deep-1: An animal's shape can tell us how it moves without telling us its whole family history.
library-dolphins-deep-2: A dolphin's body suits swimming, yet it is a mammal that breathes air and nurses its young with milk.
library-dolphins-deep-3: The breathing opening is a blowhole on top of the head.
library-dolphins-deep-4: A calf surfaces near its mother and can nurse while swimming close alongside her.
library-dolphins-deep-5: Bottlenose dolphins also use sound to find food, including high-frequency echolocation.
library-dolphins-deep-6: Sounds travel outward and return as echoes from nearby animals or objects, giving clues the dolphin can combine with other senses.
library-dolphins-deep-7: Fish, squid, and crustaceans are among their foods.
library-dolphins-deep-8: Sometimes dolphins hunt alone, and sometimes they work together to gather fish.
library-dolphins-deep-9: A group seen together in one moment may later split apart and form different groups.

library-drinking-water-deep-1: Guam’s northern limestone stores water in openings within rock.
library-drinking-water-deep-2: Rain reaching this system is called recharge because it replenishes the supply.
library-drinking-water-deep-3: Fresh groundwater forms a lens above denser saltwater, with a zone where the two mix.
library-drinking-water-deep-4: Wells can bring fresh water up, but pumping and rainfall must be considered together.
library-drinking-water-deep-5: If recharge falls during a long drought while pumping continues, the freshwater lens can thin and wells may draw saltier water.
library-drinking-water-deep-6: USGS researchers studied this with measurements and a computer model, comparing different pumping and drought scenarios.
library-drinking-water-deep-7: The model describes possible responses, rather than announcing today’s water quality.
library-drinking-water-deep-8: Southern Guam also has surface-water sources because its volcanic terrain allows more runoff.
library-drinking-water-deep-9: The water below an island therefore depends on events above ground, including rainfall and how much people withdraw from wells.
library-drinking-water-label: Where does our drinking water come from?

library-drinking-water-more-2: Wells draw from this supply, called the Northern Guam Lens Aquifer.
library-drinking-water-more-3: Fresh water sits above saltier water, with a mixing zone between them.
library-drinking-water-tell-1: Rain helps fill our water supply.
library-family-walk-deep-1: A useful observation begins with what you actually notice.
library-family-walk-deep-2: Imagine that you find a wet patch beneath a tree.
library-family-walk-deep-3: You can draw its shape and write when you saw it.
library-family-walk-deep-4: Saying that the tree dripped on the ground would be an explanation, which still needs checking; rain might have wet the whole path.
library-family-walk-deep-5: A later view could help you compare ideas.
library-family-walk-deep-6: You can make a page with two drawings, keeping the date and viewpoint clear so another person can understand the comparison.
library-family-walk-deep-7: This is an invitation to investigate, not a claim about a particular tree.
library-family-walk-deep-8: An outing can also be shared from an accessible resting place, with each person choosing what to record.
library-family-walk-deep-9: You do not need to take a leaf or move a rock to bring an observation home.

library-fish-gills-deep-1: A fish needs oxygen for its body to work, even though it lives underwater.
library-fish-gills-deep-2: Its gills bring water and blood very close together without mixing them.
library-fish-gills-deep-3: Each gill has many fine branches and plates, making a large surface for exchanging gases.
library-fish-gills-deep-4: Oxygen moves from the water into the blood, while carbon dioxide moves the other way.
library-fish-gills-deep-5: Most bony fish keep this exchange going by taking water into the mouth and pushing it out past the gills.
library-fish-gills-deep-6: The water is flowing through, rather than being swallowed with every breath.
library-fish-gills-deep-7: For example, a fish can stay below the surface while fresh water passes its gills again and again.
library-fish-gills-deep-8: A bony cover shields these delicate parts.
library-fish-gills-deep-9: Those small marks beside a fish’s head hide a much larger folded breathing surface.
library-fish-gills-more-2: As water passes over a fish’s gills, oxygen enters its blood and travels through its body.
library-fish-gills-more-3: Watch fish in their watery home with a grown-up.

library-food-web-deep-10: That can change pressure on those prey too, which is one reason a small model cannot predict a whole reef.
library-food-web-deep-2: In sunlit water, producers such as algae use sunlight to make food.
library-food-web-deep-3: Consumers get energy by eating other living things.
library-food-web-deep-4: A small animal might eat algae, then become food for a fish.
library-food-web-deep-5: An arrow from the algae toward the small animal shows where the food's energy goes, rather than which way the eater swims.
library-food-web-deep-6: One chain is only a single path through a much larger web.
library-food-web-deep-7: A fish may eat several kinds of prey and be food for several predators.
library-food-web-deep-8: Changing one connection can therefore affect others.
library-food-web-deep-9: Removing one food does not always leave an eater with nothing: some consumers switch to other prey.

library-forecast-deep-10: This offline Library stores an explanation, so ask a grown-up for current local weather information.
library-forecast-deep-2: Thermometers measure temperature, barometers measure air pressure, and other instruments record wind and moisture.
library-forecast-deep-3: Ground stations describe particular places, while weather balloons sample air above the surface and satellites observe broad areas.
library-forecast-deep-4: Combining these views gives more information than one instrument could supply.
library-forecast-deep-5: Computer models use the observations to calculate possible changes in the weather.
library-forecast-deep-6: Forecasters then combine the model results with local observations and knowledge of regional patterns.
library-forecast-deep-7: This turns a large-scale picture into information useful for a particular area.
library-forecast-deep-8: A new measurement can change that starting picture and the resulting prediction.
library-forecast-deep-9: A forecast is built from many kinds of observations, including people noticing clouds or precipitation.

library-frogs-deep-1: A tadpole and an adult frog can look so different because their bodies change during development.
library-frogs-deep-10: The change is not a move out of water, but a new body and feeding method within the same watery world.
library-frogs-deep-3: African clawed frogs offer one clear example.
library-frogs-deep-4: Their eggs hatch into small tadpoles that filter food from the water.
library-frogs-deep-5: As development continues, the young animals become frogs with limbs and a different way of feeding.
library-frogs-deep-6: The adults use their small front limbs to move food toward the mouth, while large webbed hind feet help them swim.
library-frogs-deep-7: Their flattened bodies and eyes near the top of the head suit life in water.
library-frogs-deep-8: This is why the familiar picture of every grown frog hopping onto land is misleading.
library-frogs-deep-9: African clawed frogs remain almost entirely aquatic as adults.

library-gears-deep-1: Gear teeth transfer a turning motion as the teeth of one wheel push against those of another.
library-gears-deep-2: In a simple pair of external gears, the same number of teeth must pass the meeting point on each wheel.
library-gears-deep-3: That connects tooth counts with turning rates.
library-gears-deep-4: Imagine a ten-tooth gear driving a twenty-tooth gear: two turns of the smaller wheel pass twenty teeth, making the larger wheel turn once.
library-gears-deep-5: The slower output can provide a stronger turning effect, called torque, in an ideal system.
library-gears-deep-6: It has gained force at the cost of speed, rather than creating extra power.
library-gears-deep-7: Adding an idler gear between the pair changes the direction again, so the first and last turn the same way.
library-gears-deep-8: That middle gear does not change the overall tooth-count ratio between the first and last gears.
library-gears-more-1: When two ordinary gears touch side by side, one gear’s teeth push into the other’s gaps.
library-gears-more-3: A smaller gear turns more times to drive a larger one around once.

library-gravity-deep-2: More mass gives a stronger pull at the same distance, while greater distance weakens the attraction.
library-gravity-deep-3: Earth's huge mass makes its pull easy to notice when a ball falls.

library-guam-deep-1: Guam's landscapes preserve different parts of its geological history.
library-guam-deep-2: Volcanic activity helped build its rocky foundation, while material deposited in the sea became limestone.
library-guam-deep-3: Later uplift and changes in sea level left some of those marine rocks above the water.
library-guam-deep-4: Today the north is broadly a limestone plateau, while volcanic uplands dominate much of the south.
library-guam-deep-5: These rock differences affect water too.
library-guam-deep-6: The northern limestone is porous, letting rain move into the ground; the southern volcanic landscape has many streams.
library-guam-deep-7: Those streams connect inland hills with coastal waters, carrying water and sediment toward the reefs.
library-guam-deep-8: A map therefore shows one island, but its rocks help explain several different kinds of landscape.
library-guam-deep-9: Limestone high above today's shore records an older connection to the sea, rather than proving that the hill was always dry land.

library-guam-made-deep-1: Guam’s rocks record both volcanic activity and life in the sea.
library-guam-made-deep-2: Its foundation includes rocks made by volcanoes in an island arc, a curved chain linked to movements of Earth’s great crustal plates.
library-guam-made-deep-3: Later, limestone accumulated above volcanic rock in marine settings, including reefs and lagoons.
library-guam-made-deep-4: Continued plate movements lifted rock that had formed underwater.
library-guam-made-deep-5: Limestone on high peaks is evidence of this long history of uplift.
library-guam-made-deep-6: The island was not built in one eruption, and its rock layers do not all have the same age.
library-guam-made-deep-7: Much of today’s north is a limestone plateau, while volcanic rocks are widely exposed in the south.
library-guam-made-deep-8: That difference also affects rainwater: permeable northern limestone lets water enter readily, while the less permeable volcanic terrain supports more surface flow.
library-guam-made-deep-9: Ancient island building still shapes where water goes today.
library-guam-made-more-1: Guam grew through more than one process.
library-guam-made-more-2: Volcanic activity built its rocky foundation.
library-guam-made-more-3: Limestone formed in seas above that rock, and movements of Earth’s crust raised it.
library-guam-made-more-4: This helps explain why old marine limestone can now lie high above the water.
library-guam-made-tell-2: Sea life helped make limestone above it.
library-guam-more-1: Guam sits at the southern end of the Mariana Islands in the western Pacific.
library-guam-more-2: Its northern limestone plateau and southern volcanic hills show that the island's land was shaped by more than one geological process.
library-guam-rail-deep-1: The Guam rail’s narrow body helps it move through thick grass and undergrowth.
library-guam-rail-deep-2: Its strong legs and long toes suit a life near the ground, where it finds foods such as snails, insects, seeds and plant material.
library-guam-rail-deep-3: Short wings do not carry it into flight.
library-guam-rail-deep-4: That way of life became dangerous when introduced brown treesnakes spread through Guam.
library-guam-rail-deep-5: The rail had not evolved with that predator, and its wild population collapsed.
library-guam-rail-deep-6: People brought rails into conservation breeding programs to keep the species alive.
library-guam-rail-deep-8: This history links an animal’s body and behavior to the changes in its surroundings: good running skills alone could not solve a new predator problem.
library-guam-rail-deep-9: Even a flightless bird can need help across more than one island for its recovery.
library-guam-rail-more-1: A Guam rail slips through thick plants on strong legs.
library-guam-rail-more-2: It searches near the ground for food and stays close to cover.
library-guam-rail-more-3: Brown treesnakes brought to Guam caused severe losses among native birds, including rails.

library-guam-rail-tell-3: Its short wings cannot lift it into flight.
library-guam-tell-2: The Pacific Ocean is all around it.

library-habitats-deep-1: A habitat is the place that supplies what a living thing needs to survive.
library-habitats-deep-2: For an animal, that includes food, water, shelter, and space.
library-habitats-deep-3: A good match depends on the particular animal, rather than whether a place simply looks green or wild.
library-habitats-deep-4: A forest tree, for instance, can offer different living spaces at once.
library-habitats-deep-5: Some birds nest high in the branches, while insects use the trunk, roots, or leaves.
library-habitats-deep-6: The surrounding ground supplies other resources, and the soil is itself habitat for small animals.
library-habitats-deep-7: This helps explain why a nest alone is not a bird's entire home.
library-habitats-deep-8: The bird must reach what it needs outside the nest too.
library-habitats-deep-9: One tree can be part of many habitats, each experienced differently by animals using different resources and spaces.

library-hearing-deep-1: An ear changes sound waves into motion and then electrical signals.
library-hearing-deep-10: Small movements help carry detailed information about sound.
library-hearing-deep-2: Incoming waves vibrate the eardrum, which moves three small bones in the middle ear.
library-hearing-deep-3: These increase the vibrations and pass them to the cochlea, a curled structure filled with fluid.
library-hearing-deep-4: A wave travels along a membrane inside it, moving sensory hair cells.
library-hearing-deep-5: Tiny projections on these cells bend, opening channels that help produce electrical signals.
library-hearing-deep-6: The auditory nerve carries information to the brain.
library-hearing-deep-7: Different places along the cochlea respond to different pitches.
library-hearing-deep-8: For example, a high-pitched cry and a lower bark excite different regions, allowing the ear to send more than a simple on-or-off message.
library-hearing-deep-9: The “hairs” are microscopic cell structures, rather than the visible hairs on a head.
library-hearing-more-2: Three tiny bones pass the motion inward, where sensory cells help make signals.
library-hearing-tell-1: Sound makes parts of an ear move.
library-heart-deep-1: The heart works as a pump in a continuous circuit.
library-heart-deep-2: Blood returning from the body reaches the right side, which sends it to the lungs.
library-heart-deep-3: There it releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen before returning to the left side.
library-heart-deep-4: That side pumps it around the body again.
library-heart-deep-5: The heart’s chambers fill and squeeze in a coordinated sequence, guided by electrical signals.
library-heart-deep-6: Valves close at the right moments to limit backward flow.
library-heart-deep-7: This makes the familiar heartbeat more than one simple thump: its “lub-dub” sounds come mainly from two sets of valves closing.
library-heart-deep-8: The first helps keep blood from returning to the upper chambers; the second helps keep blood from coming back after being pumped out.
library-heart-deep-9: A sound we can hear reflects moving doors inside a working pump.
library-heart-more-1: The heart’s muscle squeezes to send blood along vessels.
library-heart-more-2: One side sends it to the lungs; the other sends it around the body.
library-heart-more-3: Valves help stop blood from flowing backward.
library-heart-more-4: Between squeezes, the heart fills again, ready to keep the circuit moving.

library-insect-flight-deep-1: Insect flight begins with muscles moving wings through the air.
library-insect-flight-deep-2: As the wings sweep and twist, they accelerate air and produce forces that support and move the insect.
library-insect-flight-deep-3: A wing is not just a tiny airplane wing held still.
library-insect-flight-deep-4: The changing angle during a stroke matters, and swirling air near the wing can increase lift.
library-insect-flight-deep-5: Bees use rapid strokes and rotation to stay aloft with small wings.
library-insect-flight-deep-6: Inside many insects, large flight muscles change the shape of the thorax, the middle body section, and that movement drives the wings indirectly.
library-insect-flight-deep-7: Smaller muscles help adjust wing angle.
library-insect-flight-deep-8: Wing veins reinforce the thin surface, allowing a light structure to handle repeated motion.
library-insect-flight-deep-9: Quick, carefully controlled wing movements make insect flight possible. The same physical rules govern larger fliers, but small insects use their wings in different ways.

library-islands-deep-1: An island is defined by water surrounding its exposed land, but that definition does not tell us how the land formed.
library-islands-deep-2: Some ocean islands are volcanic mountains whose bases lie far below the surface.
library-islands-deep-3: Repeated eruptions add material until part of the growing mountain stands above the sea.
library-islands-deep-4: The Hawaiian Islands illustrate one way this happens: a moving plate passes over a hot spot, leaving a trail of volcanoes.
library-islands-deep-5: As an older volcano moves away from its source, eruptions stop and erosion becomes more important.
library-islands-deep-6: The island can also slowly sink.
library-islands-deep-7: Elsewhere, limestone formed in shallow seas can be raised above water, adding a different geological history.
library-islands-deep-8: Little of an ocean island may be visible.

library-jellyfish-move-deep-1: A jellyfish can move without bones or fins because its soft bell acts on the surrounding water.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-2: Muscles contract to change the bell’s shape; repeated pulses produce swimming motion.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-3: Yet swimming and drifting happen together, so the flow of the sea still helps determine where the animal goes.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-4: The familiar bell-shaped form is called a medusa.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-5: Its trailing tentacles help bring food to the animal, rather than serving as swimming legs.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-6: Stinging cells help jellyfish catch prey and defend themselves.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-7: Most of the body is water, held in a soft structure with a jellylike middle layer.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-8: Despite lacking a central brain, a jellyfish has a network of nerves that helps it respond to its surroundings.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-9: The pulsing bell belongs to a living animal, not a drifting piece of jelly.

library-lever-deep-1: A lever changes how a force acts by turning around a fixed support called a fulcrum.
library-lever-deep-2: Both the size of the force and its distance from the pivot affect the turning effect.
library-lever-deep-3: In a simple balanced model, a smaller force far from the pivot can balance a larger force close to it.
library-lever-deep-4: Picture a bar with a load near the support and a long handle on the other side.
library-lever-deep-5: As the handle moves through a long arc, the load moves through a shorter one.
library-lever-deep-6: That distance tradeoff explains how a lever can increase force without creating energy.
library-lever-deep-7: Not every lever reduces the effort force, however.
library-lever-deep-8: A shovel can have the effort applied closer to the pivot than the load.
library-lever-deep-9: The same principle can trade force for greater movement instead.

library-lightning-deep-1: Thunder begins with the sudden release of electrical energy in lightning.
library-lightning-deep-2: Inside a storm cloud, moving water and ice help separate electric charge.
library-lightning-deep-3: When the electrical difference becomes strong enough, a discharge can pass through air.
library-lightning-deep-4: The discharge heats a narrow path extremely quickly.
library-lightning-deep-5: The heated air expands, disturbing the surrounding air and creating the pressure wave we hear as thunder.
library-lightning-deep-6: The light and sound come from the same event, but light travels much faster, so a distant flash appears before its sound arrives.
library-lightning-deep-7: Lightning can happen within clouds as well as between a cloud and the ground.
library-lightning-deep-8: Thunder does not require a visible bolt striking land: electrical activity hidden inside a cloud can make it too.
library-lightning-deep-9: The rumble tells us about rapidly changing air, rather than clouds physically bumping together.

library-limestone-deep-1: Limestone is a sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate.
library-limestone-deep-10: A rock formed with help from seawater can thus become part of a much later freshwater system.
library-limestone-deep-11: Much of northern Guam rests on limestone.
library-limestone-deep-2: In the sea, animals such as clams and corals use dissolved chemicals to build shells or skeletons.
library-limestone-deep-3: Their remains can accumulate into deposits that become rock.
library-limestone-deep-4: The ingredients and conditions vary, giving limestone different textures.
library-limestone-deep-5: Chalk, for example, is a fine-grained limestone made largely from microscopic fossils.
library-limestone-deep-6: Travertine forms in freshwater settings, often near springs, rather than from a pile of large shells.
library-limestone-deep-7: Later, rainwater and groundwater can gradually dissolve limestone, carrying material away and enlarging openings.
library-limestone-deep-8: This is how limestone landscapes can develop caves.
library-limestone-deep-9: Some limestone also supplies water to wells through spaces in the rock.
library-limestone-forest-deep-1: A limestone forest begins with a meeting between living plants and a particular kind of ground.
library-limestone-forest-deep-2: On Guam, limestone terrain supports forests of mature native trees.
library-limestone-forest-deep-3: Their crowns form a canopy, the upper layer of branches and leaves.
library-limestone-forest-deep-4: The University of Guam’s forest atlas describes limestone forest on southern ridges and along parts of the eastern coast, so this habitat is not limited to the north.
library-limestone-forest-deep-5: Beneath some northern forests, the Guam soil series is only a shallow layer over porous limestone.
library-limestone-forest-deep-6: Roots occupy the soil, while water can pass through this well-drained ground.
library-limestone-forest-deep-7: Different ground conditions help explain why a map of forests can be linked with a map of rocks and soils.
library-limestone-forest-deep-8: A limestone forest may have tall trees even where the blanket of soil over bedrock is surprisingly thin.
library-limestone-forest-more-1: A limestone forest takes its name from the ground, not from stone trees.
library-limestone-forest-more-2: On Guam, mature native plants can form a tall canopy over limestone terrain.
library-limestone-forest-more-3: Soil may be shallow above the rock, so the forest’s underground setting matters as much as the branches we see.

library-mangrove-roots-deep-3: Mangroves can live in those conditions, where many other trees would struggle.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-4: In forests with prop roots, a web of roots stands above the mud and water like a set of stilts.

library-mangrove-roots-deep-6: As tidal water slows among the roots, suspended particles settle and add to the bottom.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-7: The roots help keep this sediment in place, reducing coastal erosion.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-8: For a small fish, the same tangled space offers shelter from larger animals and places to find food.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-9: A root system therefore shapes both the physical shore and the habitat within it.

library-maps-deep-5: A map showing a whole island must leave out many details that a neighborhood map can include.

library-mars-deep-2: Fine dust carries that rusty color across the ground and into the air.
library-mars-deep-3: From far away, the dust helps give the whole planet a reddish appearance.
library-mars-deep-4: A rover looking close up sees a wider range of colors, including brown, gold, and tan.
library-mars-deep-5: That makes color a clue about materials, rather than a measure of temperature.
library-mars-deep-6: Mars is a cold desert world with a very thin atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide.
library-mars-deep-7: Robot explorers study its rocks and landforms to investigate how it changed.
library-mars-deep-8: Ancient river valleys, lakebeds, and minerals formed in water point to a wetter past.

library-migration-deep-10: Several generations together complete the pattern that returns monarchs to their wintering places.
library-migration-deep-2: Eastern North American monarch butterflies show how that connection can extend across generations.
library-migration-deep-3: In autumn, a traveling generation flies toward winter habitat in Mexico.
library-migration-deep-4: These adults live much longer than the short-lived generations of the breeding season.
library-migration-deep-5: In spring, they begin moving north, laying eggs on milkweed along the route.
library-migration-deep-6: Their offspring grow, become adults, and continue the seasonal journey.
library-migration-deep-7: Adult monarchs need nectar from flowers, while caterpillars depend on suitable milkweed.
library-migration-deep-8: A winter forest alone therefore cannot meet every need in this life cycle; feeding and breeding places along the route matter too.

library-milky-way-deep-1: The Milky Way’s shape is difficult to study because our solar system sits within it.
library-milky-way-deep-2: We cannot send a camera far outside the galaxy to look back at the whole spiral.
library-milky-way-deep-3: Instead, astronomers combine observations of stars and gas from many directions.
library-milky-way-deep-4: These measurements show a barred spiral galaxy, with a disk and a central bar.
library-milky-way-deep-5: Our Sun lies in the disk, well away from the center.
library-milky-way-deep-6: When we look along the disk, many distant stars lie in the same broad direction, making the pale band seen across a dark sky.
library-milky-way-deep-7: Dust between stars hides some visible light, so other kinds of light help astronomers trace the structure.
library-milky-way-deep-8: Hydrogen gas, for example, emits radio waves that telescopes can detect.
library-milky-way-deep-9: Invisible light can help map the galaxy that contains our own eyes.

library-milky-way-more-2: Our solar system lies in its disk, away from the center.

library-milky-way-tell-2: The group is the Milky Way.
library-moon-deep-1: The Moon's phases come from a changing view, rather than a changing ball of rock.
library-moon-deep-10: Its far side still has day and night; it is not a permanently dark half.
library-moon-deep-2: Sunlight illuminates roughly half of the Moon at a time.
library-moon-deep-3: As the Moon goes around Earth, the angle between the Sun, Moon, and our viewpoint changes.
library-moon-deep-4: At full Moon, the side turned toward Earth is sunlit.
library-moon-deep-5: At new Moon, most of the sunlit half faces away from us.
library-moon-deep-6: Between them, we see a slice or a larger part of that bright half.
library-moon-deep-7: The cycle takes about a month.
library-moon-deep-8: Earth's shadow causes a different event, a lunar eclipse, rather than the ordinary monthly phases.
library-moon-deep-9: The Moon also turns once during each trip around Earth, keeping nearly the same face toward us.

library-mountains-deep-1: Mountain building begins when forces move large amounts of rock upward.
library-mountains-deep-2: Colliding tectonic plates can compress rock layers, fold them, and shift them along breaks called faults.
library-mountains-deep-3: In Alaska's mountain ranges, plate collision and fault movement help lift high ground.
library-mountains-deep-4: The resulting shape also depends on erosion, which removes and carries away material.
library-mountains-deep-5: A glacier moves under its own weight and can carve valleys or transport large rocks.
library-mountains-deep-7: These processes can work while uplift continues, so a mountain is not simply built once and then left unchanged.
library-mountains-deep-8: Volcanoes offer another route, building high land from repeated eruptions rather than only folded or faulted rock.
library-mountains-deep-9: A mountain's height alone cannot tell its whole history: the visible form reflects both upward movement and the many ways material has been removed.

library-muscles-deep-1: A skeletal muscle is built from bundles within bundles.
library-muscles-deep-10: Many muscle actions happen without a deliberate decision.
library-muscles-deep-2: Each long muscle fiber is a cell, and connective tissue wraps fibers and groups of fibers together.
library-muscles-deep-3: These coverings support the soft cells as they produce force.
library-muscles-deep-4: They can continue beyond the muscle to form a strong tendon attached to bone.
library-muscles-deep-5: When a muscle spanning a joint contracts, its pull can move one bone relative to another.
library-muscles-deep-6: A nerve signal starts the fibers working, and blood vessels supply what the living tissue needs.
library-muscles-deep-7: For example, bending an arm involves a pull transferred through a tendon, not a bone moving by itself.
library-muscles-deep-9: Cardiac muscle contracts in the heart, while smooth muscle acts in organs such as the digestive tract.
library-muscles-more-1: A muscle contains bundles of long cells called fibers.
library-muscles-more-2: When those fibers contract, they produce a pull.
library-muscles-more-3: Strong connecting tissue can carry that pull to a bone, moving it at a joint.
library-muscles-more-4: Nerves tell the fibers when to work, so movement depends on more than muscle alone.
library-muscles-tell-2: Many pull on bones to move us.
library-muscles-tell-3: Other muscles work deep inside us.
library-native-trees-deep-1: A native tree belongs to the naturally occurring plant life of a region.
library-native-trees-deep-2: Over time, native plants have developed relationships with local conditions and other organisms.
library-native-trees-deep-3: A tree can offer food, a place to nest and shelter, while animals can help move its seeds.
library-native-trees-deep-4: These exchanges connect one plant with the rest of an ecosystem.
library-native-trees-deep-7: If invasive plants crowd native plants out, animals can lose parts of their habitat too.
library-native-trees-deep-8: A forest’s needs therefore cannot be judged by how quickly one tree grows.
library-native-trees-more-1: A native tree is part of a place’s naturally occurring plant life.
library-native-trees-more-2: Over many generations, it has lived with the region’s soils, weather and other living things.
library-native-trees-more-3: Its leaves, seeds and branches can support animals.
library-native-trees-more-4: A tree’s value includes the relationships around it, not just its size.
library-native-trees-tell-1: Native trees grow naturally in a place.
library-native-trees-tell-2: Animals can find food and homes there.
library-night-sky-day-review-1: Our marked place faces the Sun. Sunlight scattered by the air makes a bright daytime sky, so most other stars are hard to see. They are still there.
library-night-sky-limits: An invented sky, with symbolic stars, brightness and distances. Imagined lines join dots. Earth’s rotation changes a night’s view; its orbit changes seasonal views. This is not tonight’s Guam sky or a navigation chart.
library-night-sky-limits-review-1: Make a pattern of your own. These dots are invented, so the picture cannot tell you which stars are over Guam tonight.
library-night-sky-night-review-1: Keep turning Earth and watch the stars appear to shift. Our place is turning with the ground beneath it. Stop at any step to compare the view.
library-night-sky-pattern-review-1: Choose a few star dots and join them into a shape. The lines belong to your picture. Real stars that appear near one another in the sky can be far apart in space.
library-night-sky-season-review-1: Move Earth to another part of its path around the Sun. The night side now faces a different part of space. The stars people can see also depend on their place on Earth and the time of night.
library-night-sky-turn-review-1: Turn Earth until our place faces away from the Sun. The view grows dark because Earth turns, rather than the Sun going around Earth each day.
library-night-view-deep-1: The night sky changes because we watch it from a moving Earth.
library-night-view-deep-2: During a day, sunlight scatters through the atmosphere and makes a bright background that hides most stars.
library-night-view-deep-3: When your part of Earth turns away from the Sun, that background darkens and stars become easier to see.
library-night-view-deep-4: As Earth keeps turning, your viewpoint changes, so stars appear to move across the sky.
library-night-view-deep-5: Over months, another motion matters: Earth travels around the Sun.
library-night-view-deep-6: The direction facing into the night changes during that trip, bringing different stars into view at the same nighttime hour.
library-night-view-deep-7: A pattern hidden in the Sun’s direction during one season can become visible at night in another.
library-night-view-deep-8: The stars did not switch on for the evening; our viewpoint and the brightness of the sky changed.

library-night-view-more-2: At night, the darker sky lets more stars stand out.
library-night-view-more-3: Earth’s turn changes the view through the night, while its path around the Sun changes the view through the year.
library-night-view-tell-2: At night, our part faces away from the Sun.
library-octopus-deep-1: An octopus grips with muscles and water pressure working together.
library-octopus-deep-2: When a sucker seals against a rock or another object, muscles change the space inside it.
library-octopus-deep-3: Pressure there drops, and the greater pressure of the surrounding water holds the sucker against the object.
library-octopus-deep-4: Many suckers along eight flexible arms give the animal several ways to walk, explore, and handle food.
library-octopus-deep-5: Its skin offers another tool for life among rocks and sand.
library-octopus-deep-6: Muscles stretch tiny pigment-filled sacs, making more color visible, or relax so the sacs shrink.
library-octopus-deep-7: Some octopuses also change their skin's texture.
library-octopus-deep-8: These changes can help them blend into a background.
library-octopus-deep-9: An octopus's grip does not come from glue, and its changing color is not paint: both depend on living structures actively changing their shape.

library-parrotfish-deep-2: Evidence suggests that many parrotfish target these small food makers, including cyanobacteria, rather than simply eating mouthfuls of large seaweed.
library-parrotfish-deep-3: Strong biting parts let them reach food on or inside hard surfaces.
library-parrotfish-deep-4: Another set of teeth farther back grinds the swallowed material.
library-parrotfish-deep-5: Scientists compare feeding behavior, jaw structures and chemical evidence to work out what actually nourishes the fish; seeing a bite alone cannot reveal its whole diet.
library-parrotfish-deep-6: Different parrotfish use different feeding methods, so some scrape shallowly while others remove more material.

library-planets-deep-2: The Sun attracts the planets, and their motion carries them along orbits around it.
library-planets-deep-3: Earth follows one of these paths, taking about a year to go around once.
library-planets-deep-4: The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, have rocky surfaces.
library-planets-deep-5: Farther out are the giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
library-planets-deep-6: Their outer layers are very different from ground we could stand on.
library-planets-deep-7: Moons add another set of paths, circling planets as the planets circle the Sun.

library-plankton-deep-5: Near the sunlit surface, phytoplankton use photosynthesis to make food.
library-plankton-deep-6: Animal plankton, called zooplankton, include creatures that eat these producers and then become food for larger animals.

library-pulley-deep-1: A pulley is a grooved wheel that guides a rope.
library-pulley-deep-2: When the wheel is fixed in place, pulling down on one end can raise a load at the other.
library-pulley-deep-3: In an ideal system, this changes direction without multiplying force.
library-pulley-deep-4: A different arrangement attaches a moving pulley to the load.
library-pulley-deep-5: If two rope sections support that moving assembly, each can carry half its weight in a simple friction-free model.
library-pulley-deep-6: But the load rises only half as far as the free end of rope is pulled.
library-pulley-deep-7: This is the same force-distance trade found in other simple machines.
library-pulley-deep-8: More supporting sections can provide a larger advantage, while requiring a longer pull.

library-ramp-deep-1: Lifting a load to a higher place takes energy because it raises the load against gravity.
library-ramp-deep-2: A ramp offers a longer route to that height.
library-ramp-deep-3: In a model without friction, the same load reaching the same height gains the same energy whether lifted straight up or moved along a slope.
library-ramp-deep-4: The ramp reduces the required force along the path by spreading the work over more distance.
library-ramp-deep-5: Imagine two ramps reaching one shelf: the longer one can be gentler, so the push is smaller but continues farther.
library-ramp-deep-6: A real surface also has friction, which adds resistance and uses energy.
library-ramp-deep-7: Making a ramp longer therefore does not make every real job effortless.
library-ramp-deep-8: The useful trade is between force and distance, rather than between having gravity and escaping it.

library-reef-deep-2: Hard-coral skeletons help create the structure where fish and other animals find shelter and food.

library-salty-deep-10: The ocean is not equally salty everywhere, even though its waters are connected.

library-salty-deep-4: Seawater also moves through cracks below the seafloor, where heat and chemical reactions exchange materials with rock.
library-salty-deep-5: These processes supply a mixture of dissolved salts.
library-salty-deep-6: Sodium and chloride are especially common; together they make the salt familiar from food.
library-salty-deep-7: When ocean water evaporates, water enters the air as vapor while most salts remain.

library-seasons-deep-2: A hemisphere is half the globe, north or south of the equator.
library-seasons-deep-3: When the northern half leans toward the Sun, sunlight strikes it more directly, concentrating energy onto a smaller area.
library-seasons-deep-4: Its days are also generally longer, giving more time for heating.
library-seasons-deep-5: At the same time, the southern half leans away.
library-seasons-deep-6: About six months later, their roles reverse as Earth reaches the other side of its orbit.
library-seasons-deep-7: The axis has kept nearly the same direction in space rather than flipping back and forth.

library-vision-deep-2: Light first passes through the clear, curved cornea, which bends it.
library-vision-deep-3: Some then enters through the pupil, an opening controlled by the colored iris.
library-vision-deep-4: The lens works with the cornea to focus the light on the retina at the back.
library-vision-deep-5: Here, special cells called photoreceptors respond and turn light into electrical signals.
library-vision-deep-6: The optic nerve carries signals toward the brain, which makes sense of them as what we see.

library-vision-deep-8: There is no tiny paper picture traveling down the nerve.

library-volcanoes-deep-10: A rock exposed by erosion may record underground magma rather than an eruption, even though both rocks began as molten material.
library-volcanoes-deep-2: Magma can move upward through cracks, helped by buoyancy and gas pressure.
library-volcanoes-deep-3: When it reaches the surface, the molten rock is called lava.
library-volcanoes-deep-4: Some eruptions release flowing lava, while others throw out fragments and gas.
library-volcanoes-deep-5: As material accumulates, repeated eruptions can build a hill, mountain, or island.
library-volcanoes-deep-6: The visible cone is only part of this larger system.
library-volcanoes-deep-7: Much magma never reaches the surface at all; it cools underground instead.
library-volcanoes-deep-8: Cooling rate affects the rock that forms.
library-volcanoes-deep-9: Rapidly cooled lava can contain tiny crystals or glass, while slower cooling below ground gives crystals more time to grow.

library-water-cycle-deep-1: The water cycle is powered partly by energy changing water's state and by gravity moving it.
library-water-cycle-deep-10: A diagram with one circle is useful, but a branching map with places to pause better matches the many possible journeys.
library-water-cycle-deep-2: Evaporation takes liquid water into the air as vapor.
library-water-cycle-deep-3: Condensation changes vapor into droplets, and precipitation returns water from clouds toward the surface.
library-water-cycle-deep-4: After that, the route can branch.
library-water-cycle-deep-5: Some water flows over land into streams, while some seeps into soil and travels farther underground.
library-water-cycle-deep-6: Plants take up water through their roots and release some from leaves through transpiration.
library-water-cycle-deep-7: Water can also pause in storage, including oceans, lakes, soil, ice, and groundwater.
library-water-cycle-deep-8: These stores hold water for different lengths of time, rather than passing it along immediately.
library-water-cycle-deep-9: There is no single required loop for every drop.

library-water-journey-cool-review-1: As moist air cools enough, some water vapor turns into tiny liquid drops. This is condensation. Many drops together make a visible cloud; clouds can also contain ice.
library-water-journey-flow-review-1: Water underground can move through connected pores and cracks. Some reaches the ocean; some stays stored much longer than our quick picture shows.
library-water-journey-freeze-review-1: Cool liquid water enough and it can freeze into ice. Salt makes seawater freeze at a lower temperature than fresh water. Our model skips the wait and temperature measurements.
library-water-journey-grow-review-1: Tiny cloud drops can join and grow. Once they fall fast enough to leave the cloud, they become rain. Ice crystals can grow and fall too.
library-water-journey-heat-review-1: Some water at the surface becomes an invisible gas called water vapor. Energy from the Sun helps this change, called evaporation. The water left behind can stay in the sea.
library-water-journey-limits: A simplified set of possible water paths. Sizes and travel times are symbolic, and plants and many other routes are left out. Water vapor is invisible; cloud drops or ice are visible. This is not a forecast or a drinking-water guide.
library-water-journey-limits-review-1: Choose a new route. Water can move through plants, air, ground and sea, with many different stops along the way. A real journey has no set starting point or travel time.
library-water-journey-melt-review-1: Add enough heat and ice melts into liquid water. Freezing and melting change how the water molecules are arranged; they are still water.
library-water-journey-runoff-review-1: Water that flows over the ground is called runoff. Follow it downhill toward a stream or the sea. The shape and surface of the land help set its path.
library-water-journey-soak-review-1: Rain can soak into soil and cracks in rock. Some stays near plant roots. Some travels deeper, through spaces that let water pass.
library-water-journey-warm-review-1: Cloud droplets can evaporate back into invisible water vapor. Try this path: a cloud can shrink away before it makes rain.
library-waves-deep-1: Wind pushes and rubs against the water's surface, transferring energy into waves.
library-waves-deep-2: A moving crest marks where the surface is raised, but it does not mark one bucket of water traveling all the way across the ocean.
library-waves-deep-3: In deep water, a passing surface wave makes water move in roughly circular paths.
library-waves-deep-4: The pattern and its energy travel onward while much of the water's motion stays local.
library-waves-deep-5: This helps explain how waves can arrive from a storm far away.
library-waves-deep-6: Wind is the most common starting point, but it is not the only one.
library-waves-deep-7: A sudden movement of the seafloor can displace a large amount of water and create a tsunami, a very different kind of wave.
library-waves-deep-8: Both a small wind wave and a tsunami carry energy, although their causes and behavior differ greatly.

library-whale-song-deep-2: Small repeated phrases join into larger themes, and those themes occur in an order.
library-whale-song-deep-3: This distinguishes a song from the shorter calls humpbacks also make.

library-whale-song-deep-5: A song might matter in interactions among males as well as in finding mates.
library-whale-song-deep-6: Researchers record underwater sound and compare patterns, timing and behavior to test explanations.
library-whale-song-deep-7: Males in a breeding area can share the current version of a song, almost like several singers following one tune.
library-whale-song-deep-8: Songs are also recorded in feeding areas.
library-whale-song-deep-9: Those recordings show why an explanation based only on the breeding season cannot answer every question about whale singing.

library-wheel-deep-2: Under a cart, it lets the load roll, reducing the resistance that dragging the whole cart along the ground would create.
library-wheel-deep-3: The axle supports the turning wheel, and the surface still matters: rolling over a rough path takes more effort than rolling over a smooth one.
library-wheel-deep-4: A wheel fixed to an axle can also change turning force.
library-wheel-deep-5: Pushing around a large wheel makes a smaller axle turn with it.
library-wheel-deep-6: The push travels a larger circle, trading distance for a stronger turning effect at the axle.
library-wheel-deep-7: These uses share a rotating shape but explain different jobs.
library-wheel-deep-8: One helps transport a load; the other can help turn a shaft.

library-wind-deep-3: Sunlight reaches different parts of Earth at different angles, and land and water warm differently.

library-latte-stones-label-1: What did latte stones hold up?
library-latte-stones-tell-1: CHamoru builders made stone supports for buildings.
library-latte-stones-tell-2: Each support had a pillar and a rounded cap.
library-latte-stones-more-1: Rows of latte stones held wooden buildings above the ground.
library-latte-stones-more-2: Builders shaped some stones from limestone, the rock you can explore on our island shelf.
library-latte-stones-more-3: The stone parts can remain after the wood and leaves are gone.
library-latte-stones-more-4: Look at a picture and trace the two rows with your finger.
library-latte-stones-deep-1: A latte support has two stone pieces: a standing pillar and a cap with a rounded bottom.
library-latte-stones-deep-2: CHamoru builders arranged supports in rows beneath wooden buildings with roofs made from leaves.
library-latte-stones-deep-3: Some latte were cut from limestone outcrops.
library-latte-stones-deep-4: Others used different stone, so a latte shape does not tell you its rock type.
library-latte-stones-deep-5: The remaining stones are clues to a building, rather than the whole building itself.
library-latte-stones-deep-6: In a drawing, try adding a floor across the supports, then walls and a roof above it.
library-latte-stones-deep-7: Leave the stone pieces visible below.
library-latte-stones-deep-r2-8: Latte sites are protected places, and people visit them with respect, because CHamoru ancestors lived there and were laid to rest there.
library-latte-stones-deep-r2-9: Today the latte is also a symbol of the CHamoru people, and you can spot its shape on village entrance signs, bus stop shelters and buildings around Guam.
library-question-latte-stones: What did latte stones hold up?
library-image-latte-stones: Two rows of stone pillars with rounded caps stand beside a small outline of the wooden building they once supported.

library-fiesta-gathering-tell-1: A village fiesta brings people together.
library-fiesta-gathering-tell-2: Families and friends share food and celebrate a patron saint.
library-fiesta-gathering-more-1: On Guam, a village fiesta can include Mass, a procession and a shared meal.
library-fiesta-gathering-more-2: The host village prepares food for people who come to celebrate.
library-fiesta-gathering-more-3: A meal takes many helping hands.
library-fiesta-gathering-more-4: Ask someone in your family what they remember preparing, carrying or sharing at a fiesta.
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-1: A fiesta is more than the food on the table.
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-2: Guam’s village fiestas are celebrations connected with a patron saint, with prayer and a chance to gather.
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-3: Families contribute food, drinks, money or work to welcome people who attend.
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-4: Guampedia explains that the shared meal also fed visitors who once spent hours traveling along rough roads.
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-r2-5: Long before fiestas, CHamoru clans gathered to celebrate a good harvest, build a canoe or a house, chant, dance and tell stories.
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-r2-6: When Spanish missionaries brought feast days for patron saints, villages joined them to these older ways of gathering.
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-8: Which part would you like to ask your family about?
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-9: Their answer can give your drawing a particular place and memory.
library-fiesta-gathering-deep-10: A family’s own account adds something that a picture of a full table cannot show.

library-helping-each-other-label-1: How do people care for one another?
library-helping-each-other-tell-1: Working together matters in CHamoru communities.
library-helping-each-other-tell-2: People share help as well as things.
library-helping-each-other-more-1: CHamoru scholars describe cooperation and caring relationships as central values.
library-helping-each-other-more-2: Support can come from relatives, friends and neighbors.
library-helping-each-other-more-3: It might be food, time or work.
library-helping-each-other-more-4: Think of a small way you could help at a gathering, such as putting napkins on a table beside a grown-up.
library-helping-each-other-deep-1: Caring for a community involves relationships that continue beyond one afternoon.
library-helping-each-other-deep-2: CHamoru scholars describe a value of making relationships good again and keeping people connected.
library-helping-each-other-deep-3: Help can move through a wider circle than the people living in one house.
library-helping-each-other-deep-4: Someone might contribute food to a gathering, while someone else contributes time and work.
library-helping-each-other-deep-r2-5: Help also moves back and forth over time: a family that helps at one gathering is often helped at another, and that keeps relationships strong.
library-helping-each-other-deep-6: For a drawing, show one shared task and the different people doing parts of it.
library-helping-each-other-deep-7: You could draw a table being set, with someone opening a cloth and someone arranging cups.
library-helping-each-other-deep-8: Ask a grown-up what they would add.
library-helping-each-other-deep-9: Listen for the relationships behind the task: who is helping whom, and what brings them together?

library-reef-family-knowledge-label-1: How can a family learn the sea?
library-reef-family-knowledge-tell-1: Fishing knowledge can grow within a family.
library-reef-family-knowledge-tell-2: People learn about places, tides and fish from one another.
library-reef-family-knowledge-more-1: Guam fisher Cabrini Palomo describes learning with her father, sisters and her partner’s family.
library-reef-family-knowledge-more-2: Her learning included tides, seasons and the differences between fishing places.
library-reef-family-knowledge-more-3: Guihan is a CHamoru word for fish.
library-reef-family-knowledge-more-4: Ask a grown-up who knows the sea about a place they learned to notice.
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-1: Cabrini Palomo’s account shows that fishing knowledge includes careful attention, as well as equipment.
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-2: Growing up on Guam, she went fishing with her father and sisters.
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-3: Later, her partner’s family shared more knowledge with her.
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-4: She learned about tides and seasons, places around the island and clues in the sand.
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-5: Women in that family were keen fishers too.
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-6: This is one person’s experience, rather than a description of every CHamoru family.
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-7: It offers a question you can bring to someone you know: who helped you learn the sea?
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-8: You might draw that person beside a place they describe, then ask which detail matters most.
library-reef-family-knowledge-deep-9: Keep this as a conversation or a drawing; a fishing trip needs a grown-up who knows the place and conditions.
library-question-reef-family-knowledge: How can a family learn the sea?

library-language-everyday-label-1: How does a language stay in daily life?
library-language-everyday-tell-1: People keep CHamoru in daily life by using it together.
library-language-everyday-more-1: Hurao describes learning through cooking, singing, planting and weaving.
library-language-everyday-more-2: Its family classes connect learning at school with learning at home.
library-language-everyday-more-3: The Guam Museum has also worked with Hurao on learning for adults.
library-language-everyday-more-4: A greeting or a familiar song can be one place to begin together.
library-language-everyday-deep-1: A language belongs in conversations and activities, as well as in a book.
library-language-everyday-deep-2: Hurao’s after-school program describes CHamoru learning through singing, cooking, planting and weaving.
library-language-everyday-deep-3: It also encourages parents to take part in classes that connect school and home.
library-language-everyday-deep-4: In a 2022 Guam Museum program, adults learned through classroom activities, outdoor learning and cultural workshops.
library-language-everyday-deep-5: Those examples show that learning is not only a child’s job.
library-language-everyday-deep-6: For a page of your own, draw an activity you enjoy and leave room for a word your family is learning.
library-language-everyday-deep-7: Ask a grown-up to help check the word before adding it.
library-language-everyday-deep-8: You can use the page again during that activity, or ask someone to sing a familiar song with you.
library-language-everyday-deep-9: Begin with something you want to share.
library-question-language-everyday: How does a language stay in daily life?
