library-hafa-adai-tell-1: Håfa Adai is a CHamoru greeting.
library-hafa-adai-more-1: You can greet someone with Håfa Adai.
library-hafa-adai-more-2: A greeting is a small thing to share when you meet.
library-hafa-adai-more-3: Try saying it with a person in your family, then let them take a turn.
library-hafa-adai-more-4: You can listen again whenever you like.
library-hafa-adai-deep-1: Håfa Adai is an informal CHamoru greeting that means hello or hi.
library-hafa-adai-deep-r2-2: One family in a Hurao program wrote that they began knowing little more than Håfa Adai, and a year later they were using CHamoru at home every day.
library-hafa-adai-deep-3: Try making a tiny picture story about meeting someone: first draw a person arriving, then leave a speech bubble for the greeting.
library-hafa-adai-deep-4: Who would you like that person to meet?
library-hafa-adai-deep-5: You could choose a cousin, a teacher or someone else you know.
library-hafa-adai-deep-6: Ask a grown-up to help you say the greeting together.
library-hafa-adai-deep-8: Hurao’s family learning programs offer one local example of practicing CHamoru beyond a word list, through shared activities.
library-hafa-adai-deep-9: Your greeting picture can be something to return to when you want a little practice with someone.

library-proa-canoe-label-1: What is a CHamoru sailing canoe like?
library-proa-canoe-tell-1: A CHamoru proa is a sailing canoe.
library-proa-canoe-tell-2: It has a sail and a smaller float beside the main hull.
library-proa-canoe-more-1: The smaller float is called an outrigger.
library-proa-canoe-more-r2-2: The main hull was narrow, with a triangular sail and matching ends.
library-proa-canoe-more-r2-3: Sailors could move the sail and steering paddle so the other end went first.
library-proa-canoe-more-r2-4: Early European visitors wrote that the canoes moved so swiftly they seemed to be flying.
library-proa-canoe-more-r2-5: Look for the hull, float and sail in the picture.
library-proa-canoe-deep-r2-1: A canoe's shape tells us about the knowledge of its builders.
library-proa-canoe-deep-r2-2: Descriptions of CHamoru proas show a narrow main hull beside an outrigger float, with a triangular sail above.
library-proa-canoe-deep-r2-3: The two ends matched, and the steering paddle and sail could move from one end to the other, so either end could lead.
library-proa-canoe-deep-r2-4: Early European visitors were amazed by the speed and wrote that the canoes seemed to be flying.
library-proa-canoe-deep-r2-5: CHamoru children began learning to sail when they were about four or five years old.
library-proa-canoe-deep-r2-6: During Spanish colonization, much of this knowledge was lost, so some details are still unknown.
library-proa-canoe-deep-r2-7: Today, CHamoru sailors and canoe builders are working to bring the tradition back, learning alongside navigators from Polowat, a Micronesian island where traditional seafaring is still alive.
library-proa-canoe-deep-r2-8: Look at the canoe picture and find the hull, the float and the sail.

library-leaf-weaving-label-1: How can leaves become a basket?
library-leaf-weaving-tell-1: CHamoru weavers turn leaves into useful things.
library-leaf-weaving-tell-2: Strips cross over and under one another.
library-leaf-weaving-more-1: Weavers on Guam have made baskets, mats, hats and other objects from plant materials.
library-leaf-weaving-more-2: A material can become many different things depending on the pattern and shape.
library-leaf-weaving-more-3: Try an over-and-under pattern with broad paper strips that a grown-up has prepared for you.
library-leaf-weaving-deep-1: A woven object begins with choices about material, pattern and shape.
library-leaf-weaving-deep-2: Guampedia describes CHamoru weavers making everyday things such as baskets, mats and hats, as well as decorative pieces.
library-leaf-weaving-deep-4: Look closely at a basket picture and follow one strip with your finger.
library-leaf-weaving-deep-5: Notice where another strip crosses it.
library-leaf-weaving-deep-6: For a first paper study, ask a grown-up to prepare a few wide strips in two colors.
library-leaf-weaving-deep-7: Lay one set side by side and pass another strip over one, then under the next.
library-leaf-weaving-deep-8: This paper pattern is a small introduction to crossing strips, not a lesson in making a traditional basket.
library-leaf-weaving-deep-9: Draw the object you would like to learn about next, and ask who in your community might show you their weaving.

library-family-stories-label-1: What can a family story keep?
library-family-stories-tell-1: A story can keep a person’s memory.
library-family-stories-tell-2: On Guam, people share island history in voices as well as books.
library-family-stories-more-1: The Marianas Storytelling Series brings together films, oral histories and community conversations.
library-family-stories-more-2: An oral history records someone’s account of their experience.
library-family-stories-more-3: You can ask a willing family member about a familiar place, then draw what they choose to share.
library-family-stories-more-4: Put their name beside their story.
library-family-stories-deep-1: A map can show a road, while a person can tell you what they remember happening along it.
library-family-stories-deep-2: Guampedia and the Guam Museum Foundation’s storytelling series brings island voices into films, oral histories and public conversations.
library-family-stories-deep-3: The people telling their own stories are part of how the history is shared.
library-family-stories-deep-4: For a page of your own, ask someone if they would like to tell you about a place they remember.
library-family-stories-deep-5: You might ask what they saw there or who was with them.
library-family-stories-deep-6: Draw the part they want to share and ask them to check your picture.
library-family-stories-deep-7: Add their name and the place.
library-family-stories-deep-8: Keep the story as their account, with room for another person to remember something different.
library-family-stories-deep-9: You can also choose to keep the page just for your family.

library-family-circle-label-1: Who belongs in a family’s circle?
library-family-circle-tell-1: CHamoru family connections reach across generations.
library-family-circle-tell-2: A family’s circle can include many people who care for one another.
library-family-circle-more-1: Guampedia describes CHamoru family networks that include grandparents, aunties, uncles, cousins, adopted relatives, godparents and dear friends.
library-family-circle-more-2: Che'lu means sibling, brother or sister.
library-family-circle-more-3: Påtgon can mean child or baby.
library-family-circle-more-4: Draw a few people you want on your own family page.
library-family-circle-deep-1: A family picture can show connections as well as faces.
library-family-circle-deep-2: Guampedia describes CHamoru family life through a wide network, including relatives across generations, adopted relations, godparents and close friends.
library-family-circle-deep-r2-3: In CHamoru tradition, children are deeply valued, and many people share in raising them.
library-family-circle-deep-4: Start with yourself and add a few people who care for you.
library-family-circle-deep-5: You might draw someone you see often and someone you would like to send your page to.
library-family-circle-deep-6: Leave space if you want to add another person later.
library-family-circle-deep-7: Che'lu is a CHamoru word for a sibling, brother or sister.
library-family-circle-deep-8: Påtgon includes child and baby in its meaning.
library-family-circle-deep-9: These words can be part of learning together; the picture is yours to arrange with the people you choose.

library-bread-rises-tell-1: Tiny living yeast make gas in bread dough.
library-bread-rises-tell-2: The dough holds bubbles and grows bigger.
library-bread-rises-more-1: Yeast use sugars and release carbon dioxide gas.
library-bread-rises-more-2: Stretchy gluten in wheat dough helps hold the bubbles.
library-bread-rises-more-r2-3: You can help mix and knead the dough; kneading makes the gluten stretchier.
library-bread-rises-more-r2-4: Mark the dough's starting height on the bowl and look for a change later.
library-bread-rises-more-r2-5: A grown-up handles the hot oven, and the bread is ready to taste once it is baked.
library-bread-rises-deep-1: A bowl of bread dough can grow without anyone adding more flour.
library-bread-rises-deep-2: Yeast are living fungi, and baker’s yeast releases carbon dioxide as it uses sugars.
library-bread-rises-deep-3: Wheat flour mixed with water can form a stretchy network called gluten.
library-bread-rises-deep-4: That network holds many tiny gas pockets, helping the dough rise.
library-bread-rises-deep-5: Flour also contains starch, and enzymes in the flour can release sugars that yeast can use.
library-bread-rises-deep-6: When the loaf bakes, its structure becomes firm enough to hold the spaces.
library-bread-rises-deep-7: Later, a grown-up can show you a cut piece of cooled bread.
library-bread-rises-deep-8: Look at the little holes inside and draw a few.
library-bread-rises-deep-9: Those spaces connect the slice on your plate with the bubbles in the dough.
library-bread-rises-deep-10: Bread made with baking powder or baking soda rises through a different process.

library-rice-soft-tell-1: Rice changes as it cooks with water.
library-rice-soft-tell-2: Its starch takes in water and swells.
library-rice-soft-more-1: Inside a rice grain are tiny starch granules.
library-rice-soft-more-2: During cooking, heat and water change their structure.
library-rice-soft-more-r2-4: You can help measure and rinse the dry rice before a grown-up cooks it, and keep a few dry grains aside to compare with cooked, cooled rice.
library-rice-soft-more-5: Look at their size and shape, then draw the difference.
library-rice-soft-more-r2-6: Hineksa' is a CHamoru word for cooked rice.
library-rice-soft-deep-1: Cooking rice changes more than the water around it.
library-rice-soft-deep-2: A rice grain contains starch packed into tiny granules.
library-rice-soft-deep-3: During cooking with water, those granules swell and their structure changes into something more gel-like.
library-rice-soft-deep-5: Researchers studying rice with a scanning electron microscope found that changes progressed faster in the outside layers than in the center of a grain.
library-rice-soft-deep-r2-6: One rice variety changed faster than the other two in that study.
library-rice-soft-deep-7: That helps explain why a single grain is worth looking at closely, rather than treating a pot as one uniform lump.
library-rice-soft-deep-8: With a grown-up, compare dry rice and rice that is fully cooked and cooled.
library-rice-soft-deep-9: Draw their outlines side by side.
library-rice-soft-deep-10: Let the grown-up handle the hot pot and steam.

library-coconut-palm-label-1: What can a coconut palm give us?
library-coconut-palm-tell-1: A coconut palm grows coconuts high among its leaves.
library-coconut-palm-tell-2: People on Guam use many parts of the palm.
library-coconut-palm-more-1: Niyok is a CHamoru word for coconut or coconut palm.
library-coconut-palm-more-r2-2: CHamoru families have used every part of this palm for about 3,500 years.
library-coconut-palm-more-2: The fruit gives food and coconut water.
library-coconut-palm-more-3: Grated coconut flesh can be pressed to make coconut milk.
library-coconut-palm-more-4: Leaves can become woven objects, and shells can become bowls.
library-coconut-palm-more-5: Notice how one plant provides several different materials.
library-coconut-palm-deep-1: Look up at a coconut palm from a place your grown-up chooses.
library-coconut-palm-deep-2: Its long trunk carries a crown of leaves, with bunches of coconuts near the top.
library-coconut-palm-deep-3: A new palm can sprout from a coconut, with roots pushing through the husk and a green shoot emerging.
library-coconut-palm-deep-4: Its first leaves look different from the divided leaves of an older palm.
library-coconut-palm-deep-5: Coconut water is the liquid inside the fruit.
library-coconut-palm-deep-6: Coconut milk is made by pressing grated flesh, so the two liquids have different beginnings.
library-coconut-palm-deep-7: Guampedia describes shells used as cups and bowls, leaves woven into useful objects, and wood used in building.
library-coconut-palm-deep-8: Draw a young palm beside an older one, then add something made from coconut.
library-coconut-palm-deep-r2-9: A grown-up can open and grate the coconut, and then you can help squeeze the grated flesh to make coconut milk.
library-question-coconut-palm: What can a coconut palm give us?

library-chili-heat-label-1: Why can a chili feel hot?
library-chili-heat-tell-1: A chili can feel hot even when it is cool.
library-chili-heat-tell-2: A substance in it wakes up heat-sensing parts of your mouth.
library-chili-heat-more-1: Capsaicin is one substance that gives hot peppers their burning feeling.
library-chili-heat-more-2: It acts on heat-sensing receptors, which send messages to the brain.
library-chili-heat-more-3: Spicy heat and a food’s temperature are different things.
library-chili-heat-more-r2-4: Capsaicin can also sting skin and eyes, so a grown-up handles hot peppers and washes up afterward.
library-chili-heat-more-r2-5: Fina'denne' is a CHamoru word for a hot sauce or condiment.
library-chili-heat-deep-1: A pepper can be cool to the touch and still cause a hot feeling in the mouth.
library-chili-heat-deep-2: Capsaicin acts on receptors involved in sensing heat.
library-chili-heat-deep-3: Those receptors help start messages that travel to the brain, producing the burning sensation.
library-chili-heat-deep-4: This chemical effect is different from the temperature of soup or another warm food.
library-chili-heat-deep-5: NIST explains that peppers contain a family of related substances called capsaicinoids, and that scientists can measure their amounts to compare peppers.
library-chili-heat-deep-r2-6: A bell pepper has none, so it measures zero, while the hottest peppers measure in the millions.
library-chili-heat-deep-7: For a picture, draw a pepper beside a thermometer and a little message traveling toward a brain.
library-chili-heat-deep-8: The thermometer represents temperature, while the message represents a sensation.
library-chili-heat-deep-9: Ask a grown-up to help you label those two different ideas on your page.

library-wheat-flour-label-1: Where does wheat flour come from?
library-wheat-flour-tell-2: A mill breaks wheat kernels into small pieces and flour.
library-wheat-flour-more-1: A wheat kernel has three main parts: bran, germ and endosperm.
library-wheat-flour-more-2: White flour is made from the endosperm.
library-wheat-flour-more-3: Milling separates and grinds parts of the grain.
library-wheat-flour-more-r2-4: When you help bake, read the flour bag's label with a grown-up and feel how fine the flour is as you measure it.
library-wheat-flour-more-r2-5: Raw flour is for baking, not for tasting.
library-wheat-flour-deep-1: A bag of wheat flour begins with kernels, the small grains of the wheat plant.
library-wheat-flour-deep-2: A commercial mill cleans the wheat, prepares it with moisture and passes it through stages of grinding and sifting.
library-wheat-flour-deep-r2-3: To make white flour, the mill separates the bran and germ from the endosperm.
library-wheat-flour-deep-r2-4: Whole wheat flour includes all three parts.
library-wheat-flour-deep-4: Rollers gradually break down the kernel, and sifters sort the particles.
library-wheat-flour-deep-5: This is more controlled than simply crushing everything at once.
library-wheat-flour-deep-6: For a drawing, make one large kernel and give its three main parts different colors.
library-wheat-flour-deep-7: Beside it, draw rollers and a sieve as a simplified mill.
library-wheat-flour-deep-8: Add an arrow toward a flour bag.
library-wheat-flour-deep-9: Ask a grown-up to help you read the bag’s label, then choose which part of the journey you would like to picture more closely.

library-ice-melts-label-1: Where does an ice cube go?
library-ice-melts-tell-1: An ice cube can become liquid water.
library-ice-melts-tell-2: It takes in energy from warmer things around it.
library-ice-melts-more-1: Melting changes solid water into liquid water.
library-ice-melts-more-2: The water molecules gain enough motion to move past one another.
library-ice-melts-more-3: Put an ice cube in a bowl with a grown-up and watch the puddle grow.
library-ice-melts-more-4: The cube is changing form rather than disappearing.
library-ice-melts-deep-1: Ice and liquid water are made of the same kind of molecule.
library-ice-melts-deep-2: In ice, the molecules are held in an organized arrangement, though they still move.
library-ice-melts-deep-3: Energy transferred from warmer surroundings can let them move enough to leave that arrangement and slide past one another.
library-ice-melts-deep-4: The solid becomes a liquid: this is melting.
library-ice-melts-deep-5: The little puddle around a shrinking cube is water that used to be part of the ice.
library-ice-melts-deep-6: For a kitchen observation, place a cube in a bowl with a grown-up and draw it before you begin.
library-ice-melts-deep-7: Return to the bowl and draw the changed outline and puddle.
library-ice-melts-deep-8: Your drawings can show what happened without needing a race or a timer.
library-ice-melts-deep-9: Hånom is a CHamoru word for water, whether you are naming water in a cup or in that puddle.
library-question-ice-melts: Where does an ice cube go?

library-fruit-ripens-label-1: Why does fruit change as it ripens?
library-fruit-ripens-tell-1: A ripening banana becomes sweeter as starch changes into sugars.
library-fruit-ripens-tell-2: Mangoes change as they ripen too.
library-fruit-ripens-more-1: Ripening can change a fruit’s sweetness, smell, color and firmness.
library-fruit-ripens-more-2: Bananas and mangoes respond to ethylene, a gas involved in ripening.
library-fruit-ripens-more-3: A red patch on a mango’s skin does not reliably tell you it is ready.
library-fruit-ripens-more-4: Ask a grown-up to choose fruit to observe together over several days.
library-fruit-ripens-more-r2-5: Mångga is a CHamoru word for mango.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-1: Ripening is a set of changes inside a fruit, not just a new skin color.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-2: In bananas, starch changes into sugars, increasing sweetness.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-3: Mango ripening also includes starch changing to sugars, along with changes in acidity and substances that contribute to aroma.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-4: Both fruits respond to ethylene, a gas that helps regulate ripening.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-5: Their outside appearance gives only part of the story: UC Davis notes that red skin color in some mango varieties is not a dependable sign of maturity.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-6: With a grown-up, choose one banana or mango to draw on different days.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-7: Keep your drawings together and ask which changes the grown-up notices.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-8: They can decide when the fruit is ready to prepare and eat.
library-fruit-ripens-deep-9: Compare your observations without expecting every variety to look exactly the same.
library-question-fruit-ripens: Why does fruit change as it ripens?

library-kitchen-hands-tell-1: Clean hands help us care for the people eating our food.
library-kitchen-hands-tell-2: Soap and running water help remove germs.
library-kitchen-hands-more-1: Wash before preparing food and before eating.
library-kitchen-hands-more-2: Wet your hands, use soap, rub all over, rinse and dry.
library-kitchen-hands-more-3: Remember the backs, between the fingers and under the nails.
library-kitchen-hands-more-4: A grown-up can help you practice the steps at the kitchen sink.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-1: Hands can carry germs from things we touch to food we prepare.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-2: Washing with soap and clean running water helps interrupt that journey.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-3: Start by wetting your hands and adding soap.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-4: Rub the palms and backs, between the fingers and under the nails, scrubbing for at least twenty seconds.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-5: Then rinse well and dry with a clean towel or an air dryer.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-6: Washing matters before food preparation, during it when needed, and after it too.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-7: You can make a picture strip of the steps with a grown-up: wet, lather, scrub, rinse and dry.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-8: Put the pictures in order and ask whether any part of the hands has been missed.
library-kitchen-hands-deep-9: This is something to practice together, with room to ask for help whenever you need it.

library-food-smells-label-1: How does food’s smell reach you?
library-food-smells-tell-2: Cells inside your nose help your brain recognize the smell.
library-food-smells-more-1: Odor molecules are too small to see.
library-food-smells-more-2: They can reach sensing cells high in your nose, which send signals to the brain.
library-food-smells-more-3: Smell also contributes to flavor as you chew.
library-food-smells-more-4: Gui'eng is a CHamoru word for nose.
library-food-smells-more-5: Think of a food smell you enjoy.
library-food-smells-deep-1: You can notice a food’s smell before it reaches your mouth.
library-food-smells-deep-2: Molecules released from it reach specialized sensing cells high inside the nose.
library-food-smells-deep-3: Those cells send patterns of signals that the brain uses to identify a smell.
library-food-smells-deep-4: There is another route too: when you chew, aromas can travel from the mouth toward the nose through a passage behind them.
library-food-smells-deep-5: This helps explain why smell and taste work together in a food’s flavor.
library-food-smells-deep-6: A blocked nose can make familiar foods seem less flavorful.
library-food-smells-deep-r2-7: Try a smell game with a grown-up: close your eyes while they hold out familiar kitchen foods, such as a lemon, a banana or a slice of bread, and guess each one by its smell.

library-guam-red-rice-label-1: What gives Guam’s red rice its color?
library-guam-red-rice-tell-1: Red rice gets its color from annatto seeds.
library-guam-red-rice-tell-2: The cooked rice often looks deep orange.
library-guam-red-rice-more-1: Guampedia describes red rice made with water colored by soaking annatto seeds.
library-guam-red-rice-more-r2-2: Hineksa' is a CHamoru word for cooked rice.
library-guam-red-rice-more-2: It has an important place at CHamoru celebrations.
library-guam-red-rice-more-3: Rice has been part of life in the Marianas for centuries, but the ways people prepare and share it have changed.
library-guam-red-rice-more-4: Ask your family about a red rice memory.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-1: A familiar plate can hold a long story.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-2: Guampedia describes Guam’s red rice as rice cooked with water colored by soaking annatto seeds.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-3: The finished color is usually deep orange.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-4: Rice itself has a longer history in the Marianas: archaeologists have found impressions of rice in old pottery fragments.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-5: In ancient CHamoru life, rice was valued for ceremonial foods and special occasions.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-6: Its place in meals changed over time, and today red rice is closely connected with gatherings.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-7: That does not mean every family’s meal is identical.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-8: Ask a willing family member where they remember eating it and who prepared it.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-9: You could draw their plate beside the place they describe.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-r2-10: With a grown-up, you can drop a few annatto seeds into a cup of water and watch the color spread, just as a cook colors the water for red rice.
library-guam-red-rice-deep-r2-11: If your family is making red rice, a grown-up can handle the hot pot while you set out napkins or draw the finished dish.

library-history-ancient-life-label-1: What was life here like long ago?
library-history-ancient-life-tell-r2-1: CHamoru ancestors sailed to these islands about 3,500 years ago.
library-history-ancient-life-tell-r2-2: They built homes, made useful things and cared for their families.
library-history-ancient-life-more-1: Ancient CHamoru life included building, weaving and caring for land and family.
library-history-ancient-life-more-2: Stone supports and other remains give researchers clues.
library-history-ancient-life-more-3: Early written accounts give another kind of evidence, but many were written by visitors.
library-history-ancient-life-more-4: The people living here had their own knowledge and ways of organizing life.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-r2-1: CHamoru ancestors reached the Marianas by canoe about 3,500 years ago and built communities full of knowledge and work.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-r2-2: Ancient CHamoru communities held many kinds of knowledge about building, weaving, land and family.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-2: Builders made structures supported by latte stones.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-3: Weavers made useful objects from plant materials.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-4: Family connections helped organize access to land and other resources.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-5: The evidence is incomplete: researchers study surviving objects and places, alongside written accounts that were often made by outsiders.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-6: Guampedia explains that some interpretations of ancient family organization remain open to further research and debate.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-7: A careful history can say what the evidence supports while leaving room for questions.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-8: Look at a drawing of a home and ask what its stones can tell you, then what they cannot tell you about the people inside.
library-history-ancient-life-deep-9: Their lives included much more than the materials that have lasted until today.

library-history-colonization-tell-1: CHamoru people already lived here when Spain took control.
library-history-colonization-tell-2: They resisted, and their communities were changed.
library-history-colonization-more-1: Colonization means an outside power takes control of a place and its people.
library-history-colonization-more-2: Spain began colonizing the Marianas in 1668.
library-history-colonization-more-3: Fighting, disease and forced moves caused great loss.
library-history-colonization-more-4: CHamoru people continued living and passing on parts of their language and culture through these changes.
library-history-colonization-deep-1: Guam’s history includes the choices and experiences of CHamoru people, not only the actions of rulers from elsewhere.
library-history-colonization-deep-2: CHamoru statesman Carlos Taitano describes Spanish colonization as the loss of a people’s authority over their own islands.
library-history-colonization-deep-3: Beginning in 1668, Spanish rule brought conflict and forced changes.
library-history-colonization-deep-4: CHamoru people resisted, and many were made to leave their communities for settlements controlled by Spain.
library-history-colonization-deep-5: War and disease caused great loss of life.
library-history-colonization-deep-r2-6: Spanish missionaries worked to replace older CHamoru beliefs with the Catholic faith.
library-history-colonization-deep-r2-7: Over time, the Catholic faith became deeply important to many CHamoru families, and some older beliefs and customs continued alongside it.
library-history-colonization-deep-7: Learning this history can hold both the harm of colonization and the continuing lives of CHamoru people in view.
library-history-colonization-deep-r2-9: One CHamoru chief, Hurao, urged his people to stand strong: “We are stronger than we think!” A CHamoru language program for children is named after him today.
library-image-history-colonization: Two simple maps show scattered community markers and later concentrated settlement markers, with families visible beside both.

library-history-war-survival-label-1: Whose stories help us remember the war?
library-history-war-survival-tell-1: CHamoru families lived through a terrible war on Guam.
library-history-war-survival-tell-2: Survivors’ own stories help us remember them.
library-history-war-survival-more-1: Japanese forces occupied Guam during World War Two.
library-history-war-survival-more-3: Patricia Taitano Guerrero remembered fear, but also relatives sharing stories and helping one another.
library-history-war-survival-more-r2-4: She remembered her family’s lesson: “No matter how little we had, we always shared.” We can listen with care when survivors choose to share.
library-history-war-survival-deep-1: War changed daily life for CHamoru families on Guam.
library-history-war-survival-deep-2: During the Japanese occupation, people faced harsh rules, shortages and forced work.
library-history-war-survival-deep-3: American forces retook the island in 1944.
library-history-war-survival-deep-4: Those military events are part of the history, but so are the experiences of the people who lived here.
library-history-war-survival-deep-5: Patricia Taitano Guerrero was a child during the occupation.
library-history-war-survival-deep-6: She later recalled fear, moving to find shelter, and gathering with relatives and neighbors to tell stories while preparing corn.
library-history-war-survival-deep-7: Her account includes both danger and moments of connection.
library-history-war-survival-deep-8: It is one person’s remembered experience, not a story we should pretend every family shared.
library-history-war-survival-deep-9: When we learn about the war, we can ask whose voice we are hearing and listen to the details that person chose to preserve.
library-history-war-survival-deep-10: A grown-up can help with questions.
library-question-history-war-survival: Whose stories help us remember the war?

library-creation-care-label-1: How can we care for God’s creation?
library-creation-care-tell-1: Catholics believe creation is God’s gift.
library-creation-care-tell-2: Caring for it can begin with small acts close to home.
library-creation-care-more-1: Pope Francis connected care for the Earth with care for people.
library-creation-care-more-2: In his teaching, everyday habits matter, including using less water and avoiding waste.
library-creation-care-more-3: With a grown-up, choose one small act of care for your day.
library-creation-care-more-4: You could switch off an unused light or help look after a plant.
library-creation-care-deep-1: Care for creation can begin with something ordinary you notice.
library-creation-care-deep-2: In Laudato Si’, Pope Francis describes small daily habits as part of caring for our shared home.
library-creation-care-deep-3: His examples include saving water, reducing waste and turning off unnecessary lights.
library-creation-care-deep-4: He also connects care for the environment with care for people.
library-creation-care-deep-5: These ideas can become a conversation with your family about one practical choice.
library-creation-care-deep-6: Perhaps you could help look after a plant or notice a light that no one is using.
library-creation-care-deep-7: Ask a grown-up what would be useful today, then make a picture of that act of care.
library-creation-care-deep-8: You can leave space beside it for someone else’s idea.
library-creation-care-deep-9: The page can show how your family wants to care for a particular place, rather than trying to show every problem in the world.
library-question-creation-care: How can we care for God’s creation?

library-saying-thank-you-label-1: What can we notice when we say thank you?
library-saying-thank-you-tell-1: A thank-you can begin with something you noticed.
library-saying-thank-you-tell-2: Catholics can thank God and the people who care for them.
library-saying-thank-you-more-1: Pope Francis described thanksgiving as a part of Christian prayer.
library-saying-thank-you-more-2: You can also notice a person’s kindness in everyday life.
library-saying-thank-you-more-3: Think of someone who helped you today.
library-saying-thank-you-more-4: A picture or a few words can tell them what you appreciated.
library-saying-thank-you-more-r2-5: Si Yu'os Ma'åse' is the CHamoru way to say thank you.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-1: Gratitude can start with a particular person or moment.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-2: Pope Francis’s teaching on thanksgiving names the people whose care reaches us, including teachers, catechists and friends.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-3: He connects Christian thanksgiving with recognizing God’s love.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-4: For your own page, choose a small kindness you remember.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-5: Perhaps someone listened to a question, shared a book or helped prepare a meal.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-6: Draw what happened, and ask a grown-up to help you write the person’s name if you want.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-7: You can give them the picture or keep it to talk about together.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-r2-8: Pope Francis retold a Gospel story in which Jesus healed ten sick people, and one came back to thank him.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-r2-9: He also explained that the word Eucharist means thanksgiving.
library-saying-thank-you-deep-10: Your family can choose its own familiar prayer of thanks separately.
library-question-saying-thank-you: What can we notice when we say thank you?

library-parish-community-tell-1: A parish is a community of Catholic people.
library-parish-community-tell-2: They gather for Mass and care for one another.
library-parish-community-more-1: The church building is a place where the parish meets.
library-parish-community-more-2: The parish is the people, with a priest caring for the community as its pastor.
library-parish-community-more-3: Church teaching connects this shared life with prayer, learning about Jesus and good works.
library-parish-community-more-4: Ask your family about people they know through their parish.
library-parish-community-deep-1: A parish can be pictured as a building, but the word describes a community.
library-parish-community-deep-2: The Catechism calls it a stable community of the Christian faithful, cared for by a pastor under the bishop.
library-parish-community-deep-3: People gather for the Eucharist, learn the teaching of Christ and practice charity.
library-parish-community-deep-4: Those parts belong together: shared worship and care for others are part of parish life.
library-parish-community-deep-5: Think about a parish your family knows.
library-parish-community-deep-6: You might draw the place where people gather, then add some people your family would like to include.
library-parish-community-deep-7: Ask a grown-up what they do there and what help they have seen offered.
library-parish-community-deep-8: You can leave room for a person whose work is easy to miss.
library-parish-community-deep-9: Your picture can show a particular community through its people, rather than only its walls and roof.

library-francis-creatures-label-1: How did Saint Francis care for creation?
library-francis-creatures-tell-2: Catholics remember him for care and wonder toward living things.
library-francis-creatures-more-1: Saint Francis of Assisi was a Christian who lived in Italy long ago.
library-francis-creatures-more-2: His Canticle of Creatures praises God through creation.
library-francis-creatures-more-3: Pope Benedict described love for creation as part of Francis’s faith.
library-francis-creatures-more-4: We can begin by noticing an animal carefully and wondering about its life.
library-francis-creatures-deep-r2-1: Saint Francis of Assisi loved God and the world God made.
library-francis-creatures-deep-r2-2: Pope Benedict described his care for people and other creatures as part of his Christian faith.
library-francis-creatures-deep-r2-3: Francis’s Canticle of Creatures is a song of praise to God.
library-francis-creatures-deep-r2-4: Pope Francis also tells how Francis wanted a patch of the friary garden left to grow wild.
library-francis-creatures-deep-r2-5: Flowers and herbs could grow there, and people seeing their beauty could think of God.
library-francis-creatures-deep-r2-6: Pope Francis wrote that Saint Francis called even the smallest creatures his brother or sister, and burst into song when he looked at the sun, the moon or a tiny animal.
library-francis-creatures-deep-r2-7: Pope Francis chose his own name in honor of him.
library-francis-creatures-deep-r2-8: That is one small, concrete way to make room for living things.

library-christmas-guam-label-1: What can Christmas look like in a Guam family?
library-christmas-guam-tell-1: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus.
library-christmas-guam-tell-2: Families on Guam can share prayer, songs and a Nativity scene.
library-christmas-guam-more-1: Guampedia describes a Guam family devotion during the Christmas season, with prayers, songs and a Nativity scene showing Jesus’s birth.
library-christmas-guam-more-2: Some families make a simple scene; others make a large display.
library-christmas-guam-more-3: Ask a grown-up about a Christmas memory they would like to share with you.
library-christmas-guam-deep-1: A Christmas picture can begin with the story a family is celebrating.
library-christmas-guam-deep-2: On Guam, Guampedia describes families preparing Nativity scenes for a traditional Christmas devotion.
library-christmas-guam-deep-3: A scene might be small and simple or spread across a larger arrangement of hills and decorations.
library-christmas-guam-deep-4: Prayers and songs help share the celebration of Jesus’s birth with children.
library-christmas-guam-deep-r2-5: This devotion is prayed for nine days, ending on a feast such as Christmas Eve, Christmas Day or Three Kings Day.
library-christmas-guam-deep-6: Ask a grown-up about one Christmas scene they remember: where was it, who helped arrange it and which detail stayed in their memory?
library-christmas-guam-deep-7: You could draw that remembered scene or make a paper picture of your own.
library-christmas-guam-deep-8: Leave space for the person telling the story to add something.
library-christmas-guam-deep-9: Your family can choose which prayers and songs it wants to share.
library-question-christmas-guam: What can Christmas look like in a Guam family?
library-image-christmas-guam: A family looks together at a small Nativity scene with Mary, Joseph and the infant Jesus.

library-prayer-sign-of-cross-1: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.
library-prayer-grace-before-meals-1: Bless us, O Lord, and these Thy gifts, which we are about to receive from Thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen.
library-prayer-our-father-1: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.
library-prayer-hail-mary-1: Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Blessed art thou among women and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen.
library-prayer-guardian-angel-1: Angel of God, my guardian dear, to whom God’s love commits me here, ever this day be at my side, to light and guard, to rule and guide. Amen.
